blocks.note: The checks you run after every change. No test framework: the file is a script that runs top to bottom, and the first failed assert stops it with a stack trace pointing at the line. No internet, no model, no credit spent, a couple of seconds. Run it with "node teste.ts".

assert from Node, the three message classes, and then your own code from seven files. Importing noFerramentas and comIdNovo is why harness/agente.ts exports them: it lets the tools step be driven directly, without a model and without the graph.

This line has to come before anything touches the database, and the comment explains why it works: harness/dados.ts only opens the file on first use, so setting DADOS here gives the whole run a temporary in-memory database. Your real dados.sqlite is never opened, which is what makes it safe to create and cancel watches below.

Three messages standing in for a round: your question, the model asking for a tool, the tool answering. The first check is the one that matters: with a limit of 5 the cut still lands on a human message, because a tool answer without the request that asked for it would be rejected by the model.

Two edge cases of the same function: a conversation shorter than the limit comes back whole, and a single round longer than the limit still starts at the question rather than in the middle of a tool exchange.

The cleaner: from older rounds only the question and the final answer survive, while the current round is kept whole. The expected type list spells out the result, which is what you read when this one breaks.

Two flights built by hand for the spreadsheet checks. "barata" is cheaper but slower and has two stops, which is deliberate: it makes the cheapest, the fastest and the best value three different flights, so a summary row that mixes them up cannot pass.

The tab names and order, the summary row with the right winner in each column, and the leg tab starting with the cheapest flight. Line 55 checks the duration was formatted as 50h00, which is the formatting the model relies on never having to do.
The cost-benefit rule, written out by hand on both flights: price plus 30 per hour plus 200 per stop. If anyone changes those constants in voos.ts, this is what tells you.

The Google request compared against a known string, and the comment says where that string came from: the fast-flights library produced it for the same search. This is how the hand-built Protobuf stays correct without ever touching the network.

A fake Google page in the real shape, with the class="ds:1" script and the data after "data:". Everything below feeds this to the real parser, so the parser is tested against the format rather than against a mock of itself.

A fake segment built by index, which is the clearest statement in the project of what those bare numbers in voos.ts mean: 8 is departure time, 10 arrival time, 11 flying minutes, 20 departure date, 21 arrival date.
Three flights: one with a stop, one with no price and one direct, wrapped in the same nesting Google uses. Then the real parser reads the lot.

What came back: two flights, because the one without a price was skipped rather than guessed at; cheapest first; the two-airline name joined; [null, 31] read as 00:31; the arrival carrying the next day; and the duration being flying time plus the layover, written out as a sum so the time-zone-free calculation is visible.

The distinction that matters most in that parser: "no flights" and "the page changed" must not look alike. An empty list, a null list and Google's errorHasStatus marker all return an empty array, while a captcha page and a malformed blob both throw.

Six ways bad input is stopped before any request leaves the machine: a non-code origin, a wrong date format, a date that does not exist, zero adults, ten passengers and an invented class. Each one checks the message text too, so the wording stays useful to the model that will read it.

Dates, with today pinned to a Friday so every relative case is deterministic. Numeric formats, a month name, a day-and-month that rolls into next year, "dia 31" this month and "dia 5" next month, tomorrow, the day after, next Monday, and line 119: "sexta-feira" said on a Friday means the following Friday, never today.

The same day written many ways in one loop, including numbers spelled out, then the ordinal forms, the holidays, "daqui a 10 dias", and the three refusals: a date that already passed, a date that does not exist, and text with no date in it at all.

The lock against an invented date, from both sides. A day number or a time word present in your text passes; "quero ir para Lisboa" with no date fails; and line 137 is the sharp one: the day 5 is not approved by a message saying 15/12, even though the digit 5 appears inside it.
Airports: a city with three, a bare code, an alias, an unknown name that throws, and "Aeroporto de Congonhas" with the prefix stripped.

The lock against an invented place. The fake notebook says "saio de Guarulhos para Lisbon", so GRU passes by alias, São Paulo passes by name, Lisbon passes in English, and Paris is refused because you never mentioned it. Line 154 covers the deliberate hole: a code outside the table is let through for Google to judge.
Class aliases, including "premium economy" landing on premium rather than economy, which only works because of the order of the tests in entenderClasse.

Two calls on a message carrying the same repeated Ollama id must produce two different ids. This is the bug that would otherwise delete messages from the saved conversation, and it is one line of test for one line of fix.

No agent can see another agent's tools, checked from three directions. If someone adds a tool to the wrong group in harness/ferramentas.ts, this is what catches it, because the graph would otherwise simply refuse the call at runtime with a confusing message.

The plan checker: invented and duplicated names are dropped and the order is forced, an empty plan stays empty, names are scraped out of prose, and the fallback differs depending on whether flights exist. Line 182 checks the argument cleaner: null and empty string vanish while 0 survives, which matters because 0 is a real filter value.

The test harness for the tools: "chamar" runs a tool exactly as the graph does, including the argument cleaning and the notebook in config, and "cadernoNovo" builds a notebook whose user text already mentions the cities and dates, so the invented-place and invented-date locks let the calls through.

The fake Google, swapped in through servicos. It records which airports were asked, throws for CGH and returns nothing for VCP, which is what lets one call exercise success, failure and empty all at once.

A city turns into three searches, and the error on one airport does not sink the others: the answer carries the cheapest flight, the duration already in hours, the "A BUSCA FALHOU" line for CGH and the "nenhum voo" line for VCP. That exact phrase is what the writer and the checker key on, so it is pinned here.

The repeat guard: the same search in the same request does not reach Google twice, and the answer is still built from what is already in the notebook. Line 216 fakes a notebook that already contains that search key to prove it.
The refusals around searching: a date you never said, a place you never said, a date that contradicts the weekday you named, origin equal to destination, an invalid class, and the twelve-search cap.

Analysis without any search at all, which is checked explicitly on line 242: no Google calls happened. Line 239 is a note from reality, and the comment says so: gpt-oss:20b filled every field with 0 and the filter answered "no flights", which is the behaviour the escalas_maximas rule in filtrar_voos now prevents.

The round trip sum, the per-person division, and division by zero coming back as an error rather than Infinity. All three are arithmetic the model is forbidden to do itself, so all three are checked here.
A date range stops at seven days and says so, which is checked by counting the Google calls rather than by reading the text.

The tools step itself, driven by hand. It checks the search timestamp was stamped, the search was recorded, the flights arrived, and line 265: the state object that went in was not modified, which is the rule LangGraph requires and the reason the notebook copies the search list.

The cross-agent block from the other side: the same call with the plan set to "analista" comes back as the "this tool is not yours" message rather than running. Line 273 checks the other real bug, that an airline which won no category still appears in the answer.

The watcher section starts with a second fake Google, this one driven by a variable so a check can make the price drop, fail or come back empty. The date is 2099 so the trip never expires during the run.

Creating a watch through the tool: the reply names the number and today's price, both legs were priced, and the row really exists in the database. 6000 is the outbound plus the return, which is what makes the watcher's totals meaningful.
Three ways a watch is refused: an invented date, a return before the outbound, and the same place at both ends. The last line confirms none of them created a row.
Listing, then cancelling, and the ownership check: cancelling from a different conversation is refused even with the right number, and only the owner's call empties the list.

The watcher routine, with time faked. The clock is a plain number advanced six hours per round, and checarMonitoramentos takes both the clock and the delay as arguments, which is why a day of behaviour runs instantly. monitorDeTeste creates a row directly through harness/dados.ts, skipping the tool.

First the negative case: a watch checked recently is not due, and no search happens at all. Then a price above the target produces silence, which is the behaviour you want but would never notice if it broke.

The alert itself: once at the target, with the reason and the buy link, then silence at the same price, then a second alert at a lower price. That middle assert is the one protecting you from being messaged every six hours forever.
A price that rises and falls again is news, so it alerts a third time. This is what the avisado_preco reset in harness/monitor.ts exists for, and it would be invisible without a test that moves time.

Six consecutive failures produce exactly one warning, which is the "== 4" in harness/monitor.ts rather than "greater or equal", and the watch stays active. Failing silently or warning every time would both be wrong, and this pins the middle.
An empty result is not a failure and not news, so nothing is sent. That is the null-versus-throw distinction from precoAtual, checked end to end.
If Slack fails during an alert, nothing is recorded, so the next check sends it again and the alert is not lost. This is the reason avisado_preco is written after the message rather than before.
The no-target mode: silence when the price rises, an alert when it hits a new low, and the message says "era R$ 3000" rather than naming a target that does not exist.
A trip whose date has passed: the watcher says so, stops watching and makes no search at all. Checking the empty search list is what proves it gave up before spending a request.

Preferences end to end: storing one, refusing one containing a price, reading it back, failing to delete from another conversation, and deleting it properly. The price refusal is the one that protects every future conversation from a fake fact.

The checker section. "fatos" is a realistic tool result, and the helper turns a candidate answer into a simple true or false, with a default user message that mentions a budget so the budget rule can be exercised.

Line 411 is the bug that started the whole checker: an airline paired with a duration no flight had. Then the same real duration written five ways is accepted, and a line full of small numbers is not mistaken for a duration.
The real price accepted in five formats, and four wrong ones refused, including "R$ 3 mil" and a bare "R$ 1" that a small-number rule might have let through.

Times, links and the two behaviour checks: a real departure passes, an invented one does not, a real link passes even with a full stop after it, an invented link does not, a promise to search is refused, a tool call typed as text is refused, an empty answer is refused, and an honest question with no numbers passes.

The injection cases. A price planted in your own message is still refused even when that message is dressed up as a tool result. The same number is allowed when the line denies it or talks about your budget, which is what keeps the bot able to say "that is within your R$ 4000".
A failed search has to be reported: answering "I found no flights" when the search actually failed is refused, and saying the search failed is accepted.

The opposite direction and two more: claiming a failure that did not happen, copying a specialist's "pronto" as the answer, a tool call written in a made-up syntax, and a "Pesquisando" progress line being passed off as an answer.

Saying it did something it did not: a watch claimed with no tool confirmation, a promise to alert, a preference claimed with nothing stored. And the three that must pass: the same claims when a tool really did confirm them, and a line that asks instead of claiming.

The Slack cleanup: leaked thinking removed, double asterisks turned into single ones, headings turned into bold, channel and user mentions stripped so nobody is pinged, special spaces normalised, and Markdown links converted. Line 455 ties the two halves together: a link that went through the cleaner still passes the checker, which would break if the two disagreed about link syntax.
If this line prints, every assert above passed. The absence of a test framework means there is no summary to read: either you get "Tudo certo!" or you get a stack trace.
